title: The question kept for Elijah
hookLine: an unresolved question; later tradition said Elijah will answer it
carry: an open question keeps a seat for Elijah

lines: A MOUSE GOES IN WITH BREAD.
A MOUSE COMES OUT WITH BREAD.
cards: A mouse runs into a house with a crumb of bread in its mouth. The house was already searched and cleared of leaven before Passover. A little later a mouse runs out with a crumb in its mouth.
Same mouse? Same crumb? Does the family have to search again?
This is a real question in the Talmud, asked in all seriousness by a sage, and the sages chase it around for a while. Then the discussion does something a textbook almost never does.
It shrugs, on purpose, with a single word.

teach.b: Teyku. The Talmud's way of closing a sugya without an answer. A common gloss: let it stand.
The question stays on the table, unanswered, and the page moves on. Three things to notice. First, it's honest.
The Talmud could have picked an answer and kept going. Instead it records that the sages pushed as far as they could and the question didn't give way.
The not-knowing is written down and kept, right next to everything they did know. Second, the practical side.

When a question is left as teyku, later teachers still have to decide what people should do, and they take up that work. So teyku doesn't mean nobody acts. It means the reasoning ran out before the question did.
Third, the hope. There's a Jewish picture of Elijah the prophet returning to settle what couldn't be settled.
The Mishnah, in tractate Bava Metzia, speaks of found property that should be left where it is until Elijah comes.

And near the very end of the prophet Malachi, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, comes a promise: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD."

Later tradition heard the word teyku itself as letters standing for a sentence: the Tishbite, Elijah, will answer questions and problems. Some readers take that as a play on the word rather than its source.
Either way, an open question isn't a failure.
It's a seat kept for someone.

how: When a Talmud discussion ends in teyku, students mark the question as unresolved, and later legal authorities decide how to act in practice.

games.q: a mouse carried bread into a searched house, and a mouse carried bread out. the sages have argued it every way they can. how does the Talmud end the discussion?
o: it picks the likeliest answer and moves on.
it says teyku: let it stand.
games.why: it lets the question stand, unresolved, and keeps it on the page. the shrug is part of the record.

practice: Bring to mind a question you've been forcing, about a person, a choice or a belief, and notice how much effort goes into trying to close it. Now picture setting it on a table, gently, and leaving it there.
It's still yours and still real; it just doesn't need an answer today.

wordCard.voice: Teyku. The Talmud's word for a question left unresolved: let it stand. Later tradition heard in it Elijah, who will one day answer. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: the Talmud's word for a question left unresolved, usually explained as let it stand.
